World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Food minister warns of challenging times for WA consumers at checkout
World.content:
Food security and the price of groceries are set to only get more challenging, according to Western Australian Food and Agricultural Minister Jackie Jarvis.

She said there were real concerns around food supply with recent natural disasters on top of fuel and fertiliser supply issues and cost increases.

Speaking to the WA Country Hour, Ms Jarvis acknowledged food producers were facing tough business decisions amid rising input costs.

"It's inevitable that food prices are going to go up," she said.

"As we go through the season, decisions are going to have to be made about the cost of fuel and fertiliser versus the yield return you're going to get.

"We want to make sure that people are still planting crops."

Jackie Jarvis warns food will likely become more expensive. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Ms Jarvis said packaged food was not immune to the increase in prices, with freight costs also rising.

"Eighty per cent of our packaged food also comes across the Nullarbor, so we also have issues there," she said.

"That's also a concern."

Ms Jarvis said the dairy industry was already feeling the effects of higher operating costs.

"We have I think 99 or 100 dairy farmers in the state and I know they're really struggling with fuel prices, and they're going to be facing increased fertiliser charges," she said.

Last week, the WA government announced trucks would be able to take on an extra 10 tonnes of dairy and perishables to reduce transport costs.

The dairy industry has been hit by fuel and fertiliser costs. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

"It's a small thing, but it just means it provides some efficiency," Ms Jarvis said.

"We want the economy to keep ticking over and we are acutely aware that we need fresh food in this state.

" I think we are bracing ourselves for challenging times ahead. "

Carnarvon bananas 20 per cent more expensive

Carnarvon's Sweeter Banana Co-operative estimated about 90 per cent of this year's banana crop was damaged by Tropical Cyclone Narelle.

Doriana Mangili says every part of the supply chain has been affected by higher costs. (Supplied: Sweeter Banana Co-Operative)

Business manager Doriana Mangili said a lack of supply had resulted in prices increasing by 20 per cent, taking a bag of Carnarvon bananas from $4 to $6.

"Just in the last two months due to other world events, we've had every single supplier that supplies us advising us of increases in prices," she said.

Ms Mangili said every part of the supply chain was more expensive.

She said all farmers were experiencing a similar issue, and she only expected it to get worse.

"It's really serious beyond just bananas — there's a big, broader issue out there about food security," she said.

"How do we make sure that we have sustainable food prices that people can afford, given the climate of everything else that's going on beyond just our little cyclone?"

John Cummings says producers will inevitably pass on increasing costs to consumers. (Credit: Claire Moodie)

President of the WA Independent Growers Association John Cummings said supply contracts were locked in three to four months in advance so there was not an immediate impact.

However, he said this would change.

"Look, I think you'd be very naive to think that any manufacturer or builder or business in Australia was happy as the proverbial pig on the margins they're currently making," he said.

"They would be looking for every way they could to increase their prices and recover some of these extra costs, I don't think there's any doubt about that.

"It just takes a period of time and they've got to, each and every one of those businesses, have to walk a fine line of making sure that the price doesn't go up to a point where they're turning their customers off."

He said buyer consumption patterns had been changing for some time as prices increased and people were looking for cheaper options.

"There is far more mince being sold in supermarkets than there is cut meat," he said.

Mr Cummings said sales of chicken were higher as it was one of the cheapest forms of protein.

"So all those behavioural changes that consumers have made to save money over the last one to two years is probably going to get a bit wider as the cost of petrol and the cost of living cuts deeper," he said.

"We would expect them to continue, that rate of change that we've seen."

World.title: Coronial inquest finds death of sex offender at Corella Place was preventable
World.content:
A coronial inquest has found that a supervised facility for sex offenders in regional Victoria allowed a resident to have control over prescribed medications, which contributed to his death.

A man in his 30s, whose name cannot be published for legal reasons, was serving a post-sentence order at Corella Place, in Ararat, when he was found unresponsive in his unit by staff in May 2020.

Corella Place, managed by Corrections Victoria, is a secure gated complex where former prisoners can live after serving time for sexual offences.

It is not a prison and residents are not serving a custodial sentence but rather live within the parameters of their post-sentence orders as determined by the courts.

Coroner Audrey Jamieson said the deceased was a very vulnerable man and was not at the facility voluntarily.

The report said he had ADHD, depression, anxiety and a history of self-harm episodes.

Ms Jamieson found the man's death was not an intentional act of self-harm, but a result of mixed drug toxicity.

The report said that during the time of the man's death, he was under COVID-19 quarantine, restricted to his unit and a small deck with a balcony for 23 hours a day, with one hour allowed out for exercise.

Corella Place is a residential complex for high-risk sex offenders. (Supplied: Department of Justice and Community Safety)

'Perfect storm' for drug use

An independent expert engaged for the inquiry, clinical forensic medicine and addiction medicine consultant Edward Ogden, said the boredom, isolation and hopelessness inside Corella Place was a "perfect storm" for drug use.

"In [Professor Ogden's] experience treating patients, particularly those on court orders or who had been incarcerated, drug use was often a way to pass the time, and to make life more tolerable," Ms Jamieson said.

"I find that there was a direct link between the failure of Corella Place to properly monitor and control methadone tablets entering the residential facility.

"And I find that Corrections Victoria failed to support [the man] in his rehabilitation."

Ms Jamieson also said the man was not treated with dignity and due respect, given his acquired brain injury and ADHD.

'Failure of Corella Place'

The coroner made 18 recommendations, with 16 directed at the Department of Justice and Community Safety.

Three recommendations were made regarding residents' ability to control their own prescribed medications.

She recommended that patients must disclose when they are prescribed medicines that have the potential for misuse, abuse, and dependence, and that these medications should be administered by staff.

"[And adopt] a system of dispensing medication that replicates the system or systems in place in other correctional facilities known as prisons," she said.

Ms Jamieson also said the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission should review the Department of Justice and Community Safety's training in relation to human rights.

The reports also recommended allowing for more family to visit, and mandatory training to assist residents with disabilities and to recognise signs of drug misuse and overdose.

Corrections Victoria said in a statement to the ABC that it will carefully consider the recommendations.

World.title: Cage fighter was 'mucking around' when spar turned deadly, jury hears
World.content:
A professional cage fighter on trial for murdering his best friend told police he accidentally kicked him in the head while "mucking around" during a sparring session, a Sydney jury has been told.

Bradley Dusan Fletcher was celebrating moving into a rental property in Melonba, near Mount Druitt, with his friend Bradley Evennett one afternoon in March 2024.

The 37-year-old mixed martial arts fighter, who the Crown says "trained religiously to hone his craft", was lightly sparring with Mr Evennett and showing some techniques, and both consumed alcohol and cocaine.

Crown Prosecutor Kate Ratcliffe said that according to Mr Fletcher's girlfriend, the two were drunk but "in a bubbly mood" when she left the property.

"The two mates were having a good time, but things changed," she said during an opening address.

Panicked call to girlfriend

Ms Ratcliffe said the accused "became angry" and deployed his martial arts skills.

"The accused repeatedly struck the deceased to his head and torso, causing the deceased's death."

Mr Evennett, 32, had a genetic condition known as brittle bone disease that was diagnosed when he was 12 years old.

Ms Ratcliffe said Mr Fletcher was aware of that condition and there had been no previous altercations between them.

That evening, Mr Fletcher called his girlfriend and told her Mr Evennett had fallen over and was not breathing.

Jurors heard that she suggested he call an ambulance, but the accused told her to "hurry up and just get here".

A jury heard Mr Fletcher told police he had accidentally kicked his friend in the head while "mucking around". (ABC News: Sean Tarek Goodwin)

Mr Fletcher's girlfriend is expected to give evidence of seeing blood-staining on the floor around the premises, Mr Evennett lying face down in the backyard and Mr Fletcher pacing.

She left and at some stage, Mr Fletcher used Mr Evennett's car as transport and left his body near a footpath in a nearby street.

After his arrest, the accused told police the two were "sparring".

"I promise you boys it was an accident, man," he said, according to Ms Ratcliffe.

" He's my best friend … I accidentally killed my best friend. Kicked him in the head. "

He referred to being "coked up" and panicking when he realised Mr Evennett had stopped breathing.

Deceased became 'hostile' after blow to ribs

Mr Fletcher also said the deceased "got a bit hostile" after being hit in the ribs.

"I'm a pro cage fighter, I shouldn't be doing that sh*t, you know. I should have called police, whatever, I panicked," he told police.

The jury is expected to hear from a forensic pathologist that the cause of death was multiple blunt force injuries.

That expert was also of the opinion that Mr Evennett's condition, Osteogenesis Imperfecta Type 1, played no real part in his death.

Mr Fletcher pleaded not guilty to murder but guilty to manslaughter. However, the Crown did not accept the manslaughter plea.

Defence counsel James Trevallion SC said Mr Evennett took exception to being hit in the ribs during the sparring and the men removed their boxing gloves and went inside.

But there were further challenges, and they went back outside to continue sparring.

"The hits became more serious. The tensions rose, and the tensions rose for both of them," he said during his opening address.

Mr Trevallion said the sparring was still in the context of the pair being good friends and his client did not intend to really injure Mr Evennett.

He said the primary issue during the trial will be whether Mr Fletcher intended to cause serious injury, which the Crown will be required to prove beyond reasonable doubt.

Mr Trevallion said both men were affected by alcohol and cocaine at the time, urging the jury not to "morally judge them" for their use of the substance.

The Crown will argue that the "extensive" physical assaults would lead jurors to "inevitably conclude" there was an intention to cause serious injury.

"It matters not that he regretted it later," Ms Ratcliffe said.

"That's not the time that you consider his intention. It's at the time of the infliction of the assaults."

Justice Richard Weinstein urged jurors to listen to all of the evidence, the closing addresses and his summing up before making up their minds at the end of the trial, which is expected to last for up to four weeks.

World.title: School teacher who broke student's teeth found guilty of causing serious harm
World.content:
A former Darwin middle school teacher has been found guilty of unlawfully causing serious harm by striking a female student in the face and breaking her teeth after she demanded he return her confiscated phone.

Darroch Robinson, 56, faced a two-day trial in the Northern Territory Supreme Court this week after pleading not guilty to the single count, following the incident in 2024.

Jurors today returned a unanimous guilty verdict after deliberating for less than a day.

Peter Maley told jurors his client was a war veteran with a "positive good character" who never meant to hit the child. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald)

The jury heard Robinson had confiscated the student's phone and reacted angrily when she demanded it back, calling him either a "dumb c***" or a "fat c***".

Teacher concedes he was 'angry' before 'accidentally' striking girl A former Darwin teacher who allegedly struck a female student in the face has taken the stand in the NT Supreme Court, conceding he was "angry" after she swore at him.

Defence lawyer Peter Maley argued the incident was a "freak accident" and the girl had fallen back and hit her head on a desk after Robinson accidentally made contact with her while turning around quickly to confront her.

"He didn't mean to strike the girl in that manner. He didn't mean for her two front teeth to be broken off. He certainly didn't intend for her to fall onto the table in the manner that she did," he told the court.

But in reaching a guilty verdict, the jury agreed with the prosecution, finding Robinson either intended to cause serious harm to the student or could have reasonably foreseen his actions risked causing her serious injury.

"The accused was angry at [the victim] and after she insulted him, he struck her in the face with the intention of hurting her," Crown Prosecutor Sophia Bicknell said in her closing address.

" He struck [the victim] in her face with such force that he broke her teeth directly, or knocked her into the table where her teeth were broken. "

Sophia Bicknell said Robinson was "someone with physical training from the army" who "did this because you were angry". (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald)

In testifying in his own defence, Robinson told the court the girl was an "exceptionally rude child" and conceded under cross-examination he was "angry" rather than simply "frustrated" with her at the time.

But Ms Bicknell told the jury Robinson's sworn evidence — during which he demonstrated what he said happened — had deviated from what he told police immediately after the incident.

"He initially said he didn't know who was behind him, but later when he acted out before you, in front of the jury, he told you that he struck her after she … insulted him," she said.

According to agreed facts tendered in court, the student has needed ongoing intervention from dentists since the incident, while attempts to add caps to her teeth have repeatedly failed and she has had ongoing mental health issues.

Darroch Robinson declined to comment after being granted bail and will return to the NT Supreme Court for sentencing on Friday. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald)

Chief Justice Michael Grant extended Robinson's bail until Friday, saying he was considering handing the 56-year-old a suspended sentence.

Chief Justice Grant said the sentence was unlikely to be less than two years "so I'm not going to order an assessment for home detention".

"I will order an assessment of suitability for supervision," he said.

Robinson will return to court for sentencing on Friday.

World.title: Taylor's migration plan doesn't make much sense. It doesn't have to
World.content:
More than a day after Angus Taylor unveiled the first plank of the Coalition's long-awaited migration policy and many media interviews later, there's still little clarity about what it would change in practice.

The policy's top line is a plan to take the pre-existing Australian Values Statement and enshrine it in the Migration Act as a basis for deportation. The rest of the announcements, like a new taskforce to monitor visa applications and more social media screening of prospective migrants, represent a slight ratcheting up of the status quo.

But perhaps that was never the point of the speech, which was heavy in rhetoric.

Migrants, Taylor told the Menzies Research Centre on Tuesday, fell into two reductive groups: "noble and patriotic" or "subversive and transactional". Some are a "net drain" on our country.

The immigration system should "discriminate based on values", he argues, not nationality, race or religion. But migrants from "liberal democracies" are more likely to adopt Australian values, he says, compared to "those migrating from places ruled by fundamentalists, extremists, and dictators".

Borrowing a line from John Howard circa 2001, he argues Australia should "decide who deserves protection and the circumstances in which that protection is granted".

Taken together, it's the strongest signpost yet of how the Coalition thinks it can win back voters charmed by One Nation and its anti-immigration stance.

Jonno Duniam's messaging has been slightly different to the opposition leader's. (Four Corners)

A confused message

Taylor's pitch was initially presented as a neat, three-prong strategy: put Australian values at the core of immigration policy, shut the door on unauthorised migrants, and stop extremists from entering the country.

A preview of the announcement proclaimed that screening of visa applicants' social media would ramp up from an "as-needed risk basis", as it is now, and instead become a "standard feature". Then Taylor quickly clarified that actually not all applicants would be screened, and it would "obviously" be "risk-weighted".

Taylor's migration plan faces practical questions The Coalition's new migration policy aims to increase screening of visa applicants and "boot out" people who do not abide by Australia's values.

Under the plan, a new taskforce made up of the Australian Federal Police, Australian Border Force and ASIO would be stood up to oversee the crackdown. A Coalition spokesperson later made clear it would not involve "new agencies, new powers or new laws". When asked multiple times, Taylor didn't rule out an ICE-style force as seen on American streets, but he also didn't confirm one.

The values statement would be added to the Migration Act, but to breach it, Coalition home affairs spokesperson Jonno Duniam made clear a visa-holder or prospective migrant would have to commit an existing crime that undermines those values. As it stands, non-citizens who are sentenced to a year or longer in prison have their visas automatically cancelled on character grounds.

"In order to make it enforceable and something that would stand up to the scrutiny of the courts, it would need to have an offence in law," Duniam told the ABC on Wednesday.

"This is not about stopping people from expressing an opinion.

"But when you start inciting hatred, inciting political or communal violence, inciting harm, those sorts of things, which are the thresholds in many cases across the Criminal Code, for example, at a Commonwealth level, they're the kinds of things that would trigger what we're talking about here."

This explanation was different to the one presented by Taylor, who on multiple occasions suggested the values test would be enforceable on its own.

"The statement will be going into the legislation in the Migration Act and it will be enforceable and it will be a basis for cancellation of a visa for someone who comes to this country and is not a citizen and refusal of a visa," he told reporters on Wednesday.

Loading...

Meanwhile, the opposition leader has been asked numerous times who he thinks should be deported or barred from entering Australia that currently can't be. So far, he hasn't provided an answer.

Instead, he's repeatedly made an example of the 1,300 or so Gazans who sought safe haven in Australia in the early days of the war. There are "clear risks in people coming from places like that", he says, despite a lack of public evidence that the small cohort has been up to anything "subversive" in the years since they arrived.

As a second example, Taylor invokes the Bondi terror attack. It's a potent if confusing example. One of the shooters was born in Australia, the other had lived here since 1998. The opposition leader left out those details when he told the ABC that "someone who was on a visa was responsible for the murder of many Australians".

The vibe is the point

For the significant slice of the country who believe migration is out of control and needs to come down, the details probably won't matter.

A general vibe that the opposition is keen for a tough crackdown on migrants who don't subscribe to ill-defined Australian values might be enough to tempt some of them back from One Nation, which is currently riding a previously unseen wave of national popularity.

Unlike the Coalition, Pauline Hanson's One Nation migration policy can be summed up neatly in a few words. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

"That was not a policy, that was an ideological proposition designed to win votes from a certain cohort of Australia," Multicultural Affairs Minister Anne Aly told ABC's Afternoon Briefing on Wednesday afternoon.

"Yesterday was not a policy, yesterday was, at best, a not-so-subtle dog whistle."

A One Nation-lite approach won't win over many Labor or Liberal-turned-teal voters in the centre, which the Coalition needs if it ever wants to return to government.

The benefit of being a minor party is that the One Nation migration policy can be summed up in one line: Slash the number of visas granted to 130,000 a year. The how doesn't really matter, because they're unlikely to ever find themselves in government.

And that's the other problem with choosing the populist route: Pauline Hanson has been doing it longer, can probably do it better, and doesn't have to spend any time muddying the message with explanations of convoluted policy.

World.title: CFMEU had 'hit list' of site workplace inspectors, inquiry hears
World.content:
The Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) had a "hit list" of workplace inspectors it wanted to force out of the organisation, a senior inspector has claimed.

The "regulatory capture" of Workplace Health and Safety Queensland (WHSQ) by the construction union was back under the microscope of the commission of inquiry into the CFMEU and misconduct in the construction industry on Wednesday.

It heard that capture, previously labelled a form of "institutional corruption", got so bad that on one occasion inspectors issued an unsafe work order against themselves to stop them going to construction sites where one union official was present.

Principal inspector David Cappelletti told the inquiry inspectors lost the freedom and the ability to do jobs as they saw fit "quite quickly after Annastacia Palaszczuk came to power" in 2015.

"We were micromanaged to a point where we couldn't make our own decisions," he said.

Several inspectors have told the inquiry they received calls from managers telling them to comply with CFMEU requests.

David Cappelletti told the inquiry he was aware of a "hit list" with his name on it. (ABC News)

Mr Cappelletti told the inquiry this involved having to respond to claims from the CFMEU which he did not believe were lawful.

"We tried to follow legislation, but we were pushed into scenarios where we were lurched away from the legislation to give the union favourable outcomes."

He said this was amplified when former director of construction, compliance and field services, Helen Burgess, oversaw inspectors. Ms Burgess left the role in late 2023.

"You were singled out if you didn't do what Helen Burgess said to do," he said.

" If we didn't find a favourable outcome for the CFMEU, [they] would cause problems. "

CFMEU breached industrial laws at least 25 times in 14 years, inquiry hears Former Australian Building and Contruction Commission head Nigel Hadgkiss has given evidence at the Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU in Queensland.

MOU with police

Mr Cappelletti also gave evidence there was a memorandum of understanding between Queensland Police and Ms Burgess.

"Usually, the builder would call police if they believed the CFMEU weren't there legally," he said.

"Somewhere down the track we heard that police stopped turning up or were intercepted on their way to site."

He said Ms Burgess was the point of contact for police in the regulator, and he alleged she told officers there was no need for them to head to a site as the union were not trespassing and were there legally.

'Hit list'

Mr Cappelletti said about two years after Ms Burgess started in the role in 2018, he became aware of a "hit list" with his name on it.

"I believe the hit list came into existence through the CFMEU using Helen Burgess; they wanted to get rid of inspectors that were a thorn in their side," he said in his written submission.

"I believe we had been identified because we would regularly and often refuse to partake in behaviour on construction sites that we believe wasn't legal or compliant with their entry permits in the legislation.

"So, we would push back on that with the CFMEU organiser on site, and the management, such as Helen Burgess who was the conduit between the CFMEU and WHSQ."

Senior executive speaks out

Sarina Wise began as the executive director for compliance and building services within WHSQ in October 2023, after a career at the New South Wales regulator.

She told the inquiry soon after starting, she discovered the regulator was no longer impartial and the CFMEU was influencing decisions.

Sarina Wise told the inquiry she realised the CFMEU was influencing decisions soon after she started at WHSQ. (ABC News)

She said by that point, the CFMEU were contacting the then-deputy director-general of the Office of Industrial Relations, Peter McKay, when they had concerns.

Mr McKay is currently the director-general for the Department of Trade, Employment and Training.

"It was very unusual that such operations like right of entry were going to the deputy director-general," she said.

"This appeared to be a transition from the calls going to [Helen Burgess] and because they needed to go somewhere else, they moved to him.

"I could see it was a burden on his time."

She said she advised CFMEU officials at meetings that they could phone her instead, to free Mr McKay up, but she was told by these officers they would "only call the top dog".

Former deputy director-general of the Office of Industrial Relations, Peter McKay, is expected to give evidence at the inquiry on Thursday. (ABC News)

Ms Wise said she was blocked by other senior executives within the department from moving the CFMEU from having direct lines to regional directors and executives for immediate disputes to a phone hotline for those issues.

She said this changed in November 2024 after the LNP came to power, with the union again made to use the hotline.

Inspectors issue unsafe notice against themselves

Ms Wise told the inquiry 10 days before she started in the role, health and safety representatives in her division, who were also construction inspectors, had issued an unsafe work order against their own workplace.

She told the inquiry CFMEU official Matthew Vonhoff had filmed inspectors multiple times on construction sites and shared the footage, along with commentary, onto the union's Facebook page.

"The sheer numbers of comments that would flow on from those videos that would be publicly posted … would talk about my inspectors in inflammatory ways, they would use swear words talking about the inspectors," she said.

"The health and safety representatives in my area … made the orders that would stop them from going to those particular sites when that particular CFMEU official would attend."

Employee's CFMEU conflict

She said she was made aware by colleagues, that after a Crime and Corruption Commission investigation, Ms Burgess had been in a de facto relationship with a CFMEU delegate, whose son she employed as an inspector.

She said the man — Nathan Williams — had by that point been appointed on a temporary basis to a team that "inspects high-risk projects" across the state, but she was told she couldn't pull him from that team as there was "concern about a potential claim of discrimination by association".

She said the conflicts of interests were not declared by Mr Williams or Ms Burgess. Mr Williams still works for WHSQ but in a different section.

Ms Wise said in the past 12 to 18 months the culture had improved within Workplace Health and Safety Queensland and she did not believe that regulatory capture was still occurring.

"A proper public servant should be apolitical, no matter the government of the day," she said.

Mr McKay is expected to give evidence before the inquiry on Thursday.

World.title: Workers at embattled smelter face last payday amid calls for certainty
World.content:
With just one certain payday left for workers at the embattled Liberty Bell Bay smelter, unions are calling for governments to step in and provide support.

Australia's only manganese smelter went into care and maintenance mode last year after parent company GFG Alliance failed to file financial documents, with voluntary administrators Ernst and Young to determine whether a sale is possible.

Since coming under administration, the smelter's 200 workers have been paid on a fortnightly basis, said Susie Bower, chief executive of the Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone Area.

"Unfortunately, that's how it works," Ms Bower said.

"So there are nine days left in the fortnight before that pay is, and then they'll be looking at whether the next fortnight can proceed or not.

" I know it's not ideal and certainly not for employees. "

The Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone's Susie Bower was optimistic the smelter could be sold. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Wages have only been guaranteed until April 24 after a last-minute deal with creditors, said Bell Bay Joint Unions — comprising of the Australian Workers, Mining and Energy, and the Communications, Electrical and Plumbing unions.

Workers in limbo

Administrators Ernst and Young confirmed workers will be paid on April 24, but did not comment on whether wages would continue.

AWU Assistant National Secretary Chris Donovan said the lack of certainty was taking a toll on workers, who have been in limbo since May 2025.

"We've spoken to many of our members and obviously a lot of them support families," Mr Donovan said.

"A lot of them are from George Town and it is creating a lot of stress and anxiety, not only amongst the workforce but for the town in general," he said.

Liberty Bell Bay employs more than 200 people. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Mr Donovan said he would like to see financial support from the state and federal government levels for workers facing lost income.

"The federal government has provided a lot of funding to other smelters around the country, we don't want Tasmania to be forgotten about," he said.

"[Liberty Bell Bay] provides vital regional employment and its closure would heighten reliance on imported materials, wich is something that we don't want to see, particularly given the current world environment at the moment.

" We've got a workforce that's ready to go, that is keeping the place running at the moment, and that will continue to keep it running in the event of a successful sale. "

Administrators 'can't make promises'

Sydney University professor of corporate law Dr Jason Harris said the wage uncertainty was unsurprising given Liberty Bell Bay's financial distress.

Professor Jason Harris said no promises could be made before administrators assessed the facility's finances. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"The administrators are the ones who are looking at the state of the financial accounts, and what they can't do is promise to keep the workers on if they know the plant is not operating — and we're not told that the plant is going to be starting anytime soon," Dr Harris said.

"So that's a company that has limited financial resources."

Liberty Bell Bay is Australia's only manganese alloy smelter, making products that strengthen steel. (ABC News: Owain Stia-James)

Dr Harris said it may seem obvious for administrators to keep experienced workers on, but no sale is guaranteed and current agreements may have contributed to the smelter's financial state.

"Common sense would suggest that if you're going to be buying this type of facility, you need a workforce that knows how to use the equipment that's experienced and all those types of things," he said.

"But it's also common in these types of situations that sometimes one of the contributing factors to the financial distress of the business is that the industrial agreements that are in place actually are too expensive for the business to make money."

Potential buyers 'tremendous sign'

With twelve potential buyers interested in the smelter, Ms Bower said she is optimistic the smelter can be sold rather than liquidated.

ASIC investigating Gupta's empire After years of financial red flags, corporate watchdog ASIC confirms it has multiple investigations underway into Sanjeev Gupta's troubled empire, following multiple collapses that have left hundreds of workers facing an uncertain future.

Ms Bower said the interested parties would begin touring the site with the administrators next week.

"I just think it's fantastic that we have such an interest, we were hoping that this would be the case.

"It probably surprised the administrators a little bit that there were so many interested parties and that's just been a tremendous positive sign and something that I hope the community can feel a little bit of positivity and the employees, as well.

"We've always known that the smelter is a profitable business and it can be again, we just need the right owners to be taking control of that," she said.

Business, Industry and Resources Minister Felix Ellis said the state government remained "focused on supporting the process to secure a new owner and give the smelter the best possible chance of restarting operations".

World.title: Brunei's fertiliser could feed to Australia following meeting of leaders
World.content:
Anthony Albanese has declared Brunei may be able to help Australia weather the economic chaos caused by the Iran war by sending additional supplies of fertiliser, as the two countries pledge to maintain open trade and protect energy supply chains.

The Australian prime minister, who is in South-East Asia trying to shore up national energy supplies, met with Sultan Haji Hassanal Bolkiah at the royal palace in Brunei.

The two leaders signed a joint statement, similar to the one issued last week by Australia and Singapore, expressing "deep concern" over the ongoing war in the Middle East.

Behind Canberra's political veil the mood is grim This is not over. The hard stuff is only just beginning. And it's going to get bumpy, testing the nation's resilience and its political leadership.

Both sides also "committed to working together to strengthen energy supply chain resilience, including by deepening regional cooperation, accelerating alternative energy resources including renewable energy, and maintaining open trade flows".

Brunei supplies about 10 per cent of Australia's diesel and fertiliser-grade urea imports.

Mr Albanese told reporters after the meeting that Brunei had offered "guarantees" to Australia.

"What's guaranteed is that they are not looking at imposing export restrictions on Australia," he said.

"And as we go forward, of course, in today's uncertain world, there are pressures on all of the economies in the region … not only did we speak today about existing supplies coming, we spoke about additional supplies as well."

Mr Albanese brushed aside questions about whether Australia's last prewar shipment of fuel would arrive in the country this weekend, saying the government had secured additional supplies of petrol well into the future.

He repeated that there were about 50 oil tankers on their way to Australia, despite the supply shocks caused by the war.

Anthony Albanese and Sultan Haji Hassanal Bolkiah have agreed to work together to strengthen energy supply chain resilience. (AAP: Bianca de Marchi)

Mr Albanese said there was a "great deal of consternation" in Asia about the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

"You can't take that much [oil] supply out … without having consequences for global economy," Mr Albanese said.

But he said the government's efforts to underwrite fuel purchases as well as its recent flurry of diplomatic activity in South-East Asia showed it was determined to secure the fuel Australia needed.

"We are doing what we can to shield Australia, best as we can, from the impact of this global action," Mr Albanese said.

"But we're not immune from it."

Mr Albanese will next fly to Malaysia for another series of meetings, including with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and the massive oil and gas company Petronas, to try to secure energy imports into Australia.

World.title: Daniel MacPherson on ‘saying yes to things I probably shouldn’t have’
World.content:
The former Neighbours star is no stranger to suffering for his art. But playing an MMA fighter in Beast took that to the next level.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Daniel MacPherson is no stranger to the notion of suffering for his art. “I love a challenge, I thrive on a challenge,” he says. “My career has been built on saying yes to things I probably shouldn’t have, and just giving it hell and seeing what happens.” He has jumped from helicopters into leech-infested jungles for Strike Back, gone elbow to elbow with a bunch of jockeys at Flemington for The Cup and leapt onto a runaway stagecoach as a bushranger in Wild Boys. But making Beast, a Rocky-style movie about a washed-up MMA fighter who comes out of retirement for one last shot at the world title, took the challenge to a whole other level. “I had to act opposite Russell Crowe, I had to fight like [Australian-born UFC featherweight champion] Alex Volkanovski, and I had to look as good as Chris Hemsworth with my shirt off – all in eight weeks, on an indie film budget.” He also had to train for two years, on and off, before filming had even begun so he could pass muster as a professional in one of the most brutal sports on the planet. And then, once cameras finally started rolling, he had to submit to being punched in the face by a pro. In fairness, he admits, it wasn’t part of the plan that his on-camera opponent Bren Foster – who holds black belts in four different martial arts – would make such violent contact.



“It was my fault,” says MacPherson, who made his screen debut on the decidedly gentler Neighbours, where he played Joel Samuels for five years from 1998. “I was supposed to have my hands up and I didn’t. What’s the first rule of fighting? Protect yourself at all times. It was all my fault.” Related Article Australian film How a model and reality-TV star turned to film to tell the raw story of his youth The fight scenes were choreographed by Foster, and he, MacPherson says, “was millimetre perfect”. Not so the leading man. “I was supposed to have my hands somewhere and I didn’t, and I just felt this sharp crack.” The punch had broken his nose. But not for a moment did MacPherson consider throwing in the towel. “I went, ‘Oh, hang on. I may just need a second’,” he told the crew. “My eyes were watering, I did a lap of the octagon [the fighting cage], and jumped back in. ‘All right, let’s go.’ I really won’t make that mistake twice.” Nor was it the only injury he suffered. By the time the final fight scenes for the film were being shot in a real MMA stadium (Bangkok’s Impact Arena), “I had a broken nose, I’d torn my adductor [groin muscle] off the bone, I’d fractured my pelvis and they had to cover up my black eyes to put on the fake black eyes and the fake prosthetics”. In Beast, MacPherson plays Patton James. We meet him as he’s about to enter the ring for a title bout. Crippling doubt has set in and he’s vomiting in the dressing room. Enter Russell Crowe as his trainer, Sammy, with one of the most rousing motivational speeches you’ll ever see. As opening scenes go, it’s a knockout.



The action quickly flashes forward a decade, and a markedly less-ripped Patton is now working as a fisherman on a deep-sea trawler, being paid a pittance – or not at all, depending on the catch and the whim of the A-hole boat captain – and struggling to keep his family afloat. He takes his responsibilities seriously, though; he wants to be a good husband to Luciana (Kelly Gale) and support her while she finishes her degree, and he wants to be a good father to their son. Fighting would offer a big pay day and make all of that so much easier, but he’s promised Luciana not to go back in the ring, because it’s too dangerous. Of course, it’s a promise he’s destined, eventually, to break. The fight scenes were tightly choreographed by Bren Foster, left. But that didn’t mean they didn’t hurt. Stan Beast (which had been called The Beast In Me – after the Johnny Cash song that’s covered in the closing credits by Russell Crowe and his band Indoor Garden Party – until a certain Netflix series starring Claire Danes and Matthew Rhys came along) may not win prizes for originality. But it could snaffle a few for the unflinching flesh-on-flesh realism of its fight sequences. MacPherson was working on the war movie Land of Bad on the Gold Coast in 2022, along with Crowe and Liam Hemsworth and his brother, Luke, when that film’s writer, American David Frigerio, said he had another project that might be of interest. “He gave me the script [for Beast] and said, ’I’ve watched you and Russell work over the last two weeks, and you’d be perfect for these characters I’ve got in this MMA film,” MacPherson recalls. “I read the script and it was fantastic, except it was set in Buffalo, New York, and I didn’t know the first thing about what life was like working in a steel factory in Buffalo, New York. “And then Tyler Atkins came on as director and Tyler didn’t know much about what life was like in Buffalo, New York, either. But we did know a lot about growing up in places like Newcastle and Wollongong.”



But while Atkins – the winner of the first season of The Amazing Race Australia, who made his feature debut with the semi-autobiographical surf movie Bosch & Rockit in 2022 – found plenty to like in the script, he also saw its shortcomings. “I turned it down a couple of times because it was originally set in America, and obviously there have been stories like this before,” he says. The breakthrough came after he spoke with Luke Hemsworth, whom he calls “one of my dear friends” (he was the adult lead in Bosch & Rockit and has a small role in Beast) about “certain issues” he had with the story. “And he told me, ‘you’re never going to get a script that you absolutely love, but as a filmmaker, if you can see things you like, you can start injecting them’. And that was just a really good a-ha moment for me.” With MacPherson on board, Atkins started retooling the story, moving the action to Port Kembla. And when Crowe committed, the Oscar winner gave the script a pass of his own (enough to earn a co-writer credit). Amy Shark and Russell Crowe as the daughter-father trainers who coach Patton back to contention. Stan Atkins infused the story not just with a strong sense of Australianness, but also with the kinds of themes he was passionate about. “I’m pro-relationship, I’m pro-family, pro-forgiveness, and pro-men chasing their dreams … I worked really hard to shape a story that could show true masculinity.” In this era of the so-called manosphere, Atkins knows any talk of masculinity can be problematic. “It’s a slippery slope,” he says. “But we have to be able to have conscious discussions about what a man is.



“To me, masculinity is not a man who can break down a wall,” he continues. “Masculinity is a man who can have his heart broken and rebuild and come back stronger and better. There’s a big push in this world that’s toxic masculinity, but no one ever says anything about good male role models. And I wanted to really show the world – and Dan was a big part of this – what a true man is. “A man is someone who can grow and have an honest life and doesn’t fuck people over, is a responsible father and a great husband, who works hard. I’m talking about men that are heart-centred and understand emotions and are emotionally intelligent and show up.” And know how to land a punch, when necessary. Atkins, who lives in Byron Bay with his wife and daughters, is a slender, gentle, spiritual soul. But he was drawn to the world of fighters because “they’re men who can protect communities, protect women and protect children from things coming into their town or their village, they can step up and say, ‘no, that’s wrong’.” He’s met plenty of fighters, he says, and the best of them “are not out there smashing people. They’re actually very beautiful people. It’s a meditation, and they’re very grounded. If push comes to shove, they’ll stand up and protect people. And that, to me, is a real, true man. He doesn’t live in that place, but he goes to that place if he needs to, then he comes back to being vulnerable and centred, and can still have these heart-to-heart talks that men need to learn how to have.” Atkins on the set of his second feature. Stan That’s a lot of weight to put on a fight movie, perhaps. And there were times when the weight became almost unbearable for Atkins.

World.title: Lesbian activists claim win in push to exclude trans women from events
World.content:
NationalNSWCourts Lesbian activists claim win in push to exclude trans women from events Jack Gramenz and Michaela Whitbourn April 15, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

A lesbian activist group seeking to exclude transgender women from public events said it will continue its push for an exemption from discrimination laws after what it called a “win” in the Federal Court. The Lesbian Action Group applied in 2023 to the Australian Human Rights Commission for a five-year exemption from Commonwealth sex discrimination laws to allow them to hold public events for “lesbians born female only”. Lesbian Action Group committee member Carole Ann, pictured in August 2023. Wayne Taylor The laws make it unlawful to discriminate on the grounds of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity in the provision of goods, services and facilities. The commission rejected the application for the exemption in October, and the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed the decision in January last year.



In a decision on Wednesday, Federal Court Justice Mark Moshinsky set aside the tribunal’s decision and ordered it to consider the case afresh after finding a “material” error in its reasoning. The group welcomed the judgment on social media platform X. “We have won the right to have the judgment from the tribunal set aside and be permitted to go back to the tribunal to continue our fight for an exemption to the Sex Discrimination Act to be able to have a public gathering for women just like us and only us.” “The fight isn’t over and the law hasn’t changed but today was a major win for us,” the group said in another post. Moshinsky said the group “sought the exemption so that it could hold regular public events for lesbians born female only”, starting with an International Lesbian Day event in St Kilda, Melbourne.



The commission denied the exemption in October that year, three days before the event was scheduled. Representatives from the Lesbian Action Group and Women’s Rights Network Australia outside the Federal Court in August 2024. Sitthixay Ditthavong Moshinsky said the tribunal had taken “too narrow a view of the scope” of the available exemption power in its 2025 ruling. “While an exemption may be granted in circumstances that could be described as ‘positive discrimination’, the power to grant an exemption is not limited to such cases,” Moshinsky said. “An exemption may be granted which serves other interests notwithstanding that it permits a person to engage in acts of discrimination on the ground of sex etc that would otherwise be prohibited.”



Katie Green, CEO of the Inner City Legal Centre in Sydney, advocates regularly for the rights of trans people. She warned that lobbying to exclude trans women was an “own goal” for the LGBTIQ community as a whole. “If we see a winding back of trans rights in Australia, it’s going to be lesbian and gay rights that other powerful lobby groups will come after next,” Green said. “At the ICLC we do work with lots of younger groups that are so much more open about their identity. “So many younger trans women and lesbians are in fact attracted to one another because of the shared struggle.” She was concerned the litigation, and cases like it, created a culture in which people felt emboldened to aim “hateful and often violent” behaviour towards the trans community.



“So many ICLC cases, big and small, revolve around the rights of trans people to exist in public spaces,” she said. “What happens next? Then we have things like toilet bans potentially being next on the agenda.” Sydney woman May May, who is trans and attracted to women, said the views of the Lesbian Action Group were not representative of the wider LGBTIQ community. She was “doubtful that any trans women engage in that space at all”. “I think this group is mostly an outlier within the queer community,” May said.



“If you love women, there will be trans women you love and there will be cis women you love.” Having pockets within the LGBTIQ community attacking trans women was ultimately “self-defeating”, she said, because it created an environment in which the queer community as a whole could be marginalised. World.title: ‘Dubbed a liar’: Power to appeal after Zak Butters’ family seethes over umpire abuse fine
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Dubbed a liar’: Power to appeal after Zak Butters’ family seethes over umpire abuse fine Jon Pierik Updated April 15, 2026 — 7:00pm ,first published 1:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

The AFL tribunal argued it was implausible that field umpire Nick Foot would have claimed he had been abused if he hadn’t been, as the division between players and umpires became even wider in the aftermath of the Zak Butters controversy. The league released its written findings on Wednesday, Butters having been fined $1500 for alleged abusive or insulting language towards an official in Sunday’s clash between the Power and St Kilda. Port Adelaide star Zak Butters was dumbfounded when the umpire paid a 50-metre penalty against him on Sunday. AFL Photos The guilty finding left Butters and his family seething, with Power chairman David Koch declaring Butters had effectively been “dubbed a liar”, and the club later announcing it would appeal the verdict. “The tribunal last night upheld the charge, resulting in a $1,500 fine. The club believes strongly in Butters’ account of events and will formally contest the verdict,” the Power said in a statement.



“The AFL will confirm the date and time of the appeal hearing in due course.” The case featured conflicting evidence from Foot, Butters and another Power star Ollie Wines. Experienced umpire Foot alleged that he heard the Power player say, “How much are they paying you?” before he paid a 50-metre penalty and reported Butters. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 Inside the shambolic Zak Butters tribunal process that failed at every step Peter Ryan Sports reporter The Power midfielder claimed he had made only one comment to Foot, and that had not been the key statement alleged. In the judgment handed down by tribunal chair Renee Enbom, KC, and fellow panellists, former players Jason Johnson and Darren Gaspar, the panel said: “On a careful consideration of the whole of the evidence, the tribunal was satisfied to the requisite standard that Mr Butters made the offending comment.



“It is implausible that Mr Foot would invent the offending comment, and it was not put to him that he had done so. It was put to him that there were several distractions and that he had misheard what Mr Butters said. We also consider that to be implausible. “It is implausible that Mr Foot misheard the words “Surely that’s not a free kick” as “How much are they paying you?” None of the words that Mr Butters said he spoke are any of the words that Mr Foot believes he heard. Mr Foot was certain as to what he heard, the two men were standing close to one another and Mr Foot responded without hesitation in giving a 50-metre penalty and then shortly thereafter telling Mr Butters that he was being reported. “We reject Mr Butters evidence that he only made one comment about the free kick against player Sweet (“Surely that’s not a free kick” ) and that his only comment was made after Mr Foot blew his whistle to move the ball on. The evidence as to him only making that one comment is contrary to the evidence of Mr Foot, who said that Mr Butters made more than one comment.” View post on X The panel found Butters had made more than one comment to Foot, and it was understandable that Wines, who had declared that he was “100 per cent” certain Butters had not made the offending comment, had not heard this.



“It is not surprising that Mr Wines did not hear the offending comment. Mr Foot’s unchallenged evidence was that Mr Butters made the offending comment at a lower volume than his earlier comments,” the panel said. “Mr Wines was at least 1.5 metres away from Mr Butters. The distance and positioning made it difficult for Mr Butters himself to hear what Mr Wines was saying to Mr Foot about his umpiring decision.” Loading The panel said Butters’ long history of sanctions was also “relevant” in its finding. “Mr Butters did not use expletives and while the offending comment was insulting and should not have been made, it can be described as a sledge made among other dissenting comments by players to Mr Foot which might have separately warranted a 50-metre penalty,” the panel said.



“However, it is also relevant that this is far from the first time that Mr Butters has committed a reportable offence during his career. He has committed well over a dozen reportable offences over the last eight seasons.” Butters has now been sanctioned 22 times through his career, the fines totalling $51,625. Took offence: Umpire Nick Foot in action on Sunday. AFL Photos Koch said ealier: “Zak is a competitor, but he’s one of the nicest blokes you could ever meet. And you know he’s incredibly angry with the outcome because, you know, quite rightly, he believes that he’s been dubbed a liar in this. “And, you know, the bloke has enormous pride and integrity of his values… I can tell you, his family, his mum and dad, equally are as devastated and angry.



“We put up a witness, the league’s best and fairest, a former Brownlow Medal winner, but the decision took none of that into account, and seemed to focus on semantics.” AFL Umpires Association chief executive Rob Kerr said Foot had handled the issue appropriately. “In the case of the Zak Butters report, Nick Foot is adamant that his integrity was questioned, and he acted appropriately by reporting the incident,” Kerr said. “Nick Foot was subject to multiple pointed criticisms of his character when he did not engage with Zak Butters at the conclusion of the game. Those criticisms were made without an understanding that an umpire is prohibited by the Laws of the Game from speaking to a player they have reported.”



Kerr said Foot had not wavered in his evidence, and had since been subjected to malicious online trolling. “While debate about the decision continues, Nick Foot has never wavered from his account. His response to what he perceived was said was entirely consistent with the expectations placed on umpires charged with protecting the game’s integrity, and he has behaved appropriately through each step of this process at the cost of significant personal discomfort, particularly with some of the online vitriol,” Kerr said. That the release of the tribunal’s written findings were delayed from Tuesday evening’s hearing, which Enbom said had to end by 5.45pm, prompted former Collingwood president Eddie McGuire to declare the drawnout process was not good enough. Johnson also briefly left the virtual hearing to transfer to his phone and was in a car as the hearing came to an end. Concern was expressed that Johnson had dropped out of the video link, but the former Essendon player assured the hearing he had not missed any of the evidence.



However, the AFL did speak privately to Johnson on Wednesday about his movements during the meeting, with the tribunal panellist admitting it was not a good look. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Do you really need to know everything about your partner?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSex & relationships Do you really need to know everything about your partner? Lauren Ironmonger April 15, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

What do you do when the person you thought you loved isn’t who you thought they were? And how well should – and can – we truly know the people we love? These are the central questions plaguing Emma (Zendaya) and Charlie (Robert Pattinson) in A24’s The Drama, whose impending engagement is thrown into a tailspin after Emma reveals the worst thing she’s ever done. Robert Pattinson and Zendaya star in A24’s The Drama. AP Speaking on the New York Times′ Modern Love podcast, the co-stars (both in long-term relationships of their own) were asked to weigh in on how much you need to know before committing to someone. While Pattinson was an advocate for surprise (“I think you kind of suffocate a relationship if you’re saying, I need to know everything about your past”), Zendaya felt it was important to know someone “at the core”.



While the secret at the heart of The Drama may be extreme, the questions it asks – about what it is to love someone in spite of their past, and the impulse to know everything about those we love – are deeply human. Is total transparency necessary in relationships? Dr Tim Dean, a senior philosopher at The Ethics Centre, says truth is a core tenet of moral philosophy. However, he also acknowledges intimate relationships are inherently vulnerable. “Sometimes that means people aren’t necessarily ready for, or able to understand or interpret the truth, and so sometimes we do need a little bit of privacy,” he says. “Ethically, you wouldn’t withhold information for self-interested purposes. You’re not trying to deceive somebody. But if your intention is to help and support your partner, then I think that is actually quite reasonable.”



Editor's pick Milano Cortina 2026 This Olympian told the world. But is there a ‘right’ way to confess your affair? Dean gives the example of past relationships and how it’s not always helpful to talk in detail about them with a new partner. “Honesty is a very important principle underlying intimate relationships,” agrees Dr Rowan Burckhardt, clinical psychologist and founder of the Sydney Couples Counselling Centre. However, he says there are some cases when this can bristle against other principles, like “emotional awareness, compassion and empathy”. This is particularly true for instances from one’s past. Still, he says, “you have to be careful this doesn’t become a justification for destructive behaviour or withholding important information,” like not telling a partner about infidelity.



Psychology researcher Dr Raquel Peel points out that keeping secrets is extremely common – the average person has 13 at any one time, according to previous studies. “It’s actually more about whether that secret keeps you preoccupied to a point where you feel like, ‘if they find out that I’m keeping this secret, they’re not going to love me, or they’re going to reject me, or think differently about me’,” says Peel, referencing research on how secret keeping affects well-being. “Because we don’t always keep secrets intentionally. It’s just part of being human – we have our thoughts, and we are not sharing everything that comes across our mind.” The Drama asks whether you need to know everything about someone before committing to them. AP Can you ever truly know someone?



It’s a question that philosophers, lovers and laypeople have pondered for millennia: is it possible to ever truly, fully know someone? The short (and rather unsatisfying) answer, says Dean, is no. “We can never truly know ourselves. A lot of our own behaviour and the way we encounter the world is unconscious... And we know that we create stories about ourselves,” he says. “So if we think about how difficult it is for us to understand ourselves, it’s even harder to understand other people – what truly goes on in their minds. And while that can be frustrating, it can also be a source of surprise. “This is both the wonder and the pain of humanity in trying to find a relationship where our weirdness and our uniqueness can somehow become compatible with somebody else’s.”



Editor's pick Red carpet Something borrowed, something blue: Zendaya raids Cate Blanchett’s closet Given these limitations, determining someone’s moral character can be tricky. “We automatically judge people’s character all the time,” says Dean, pointing to “attribution bias”, the concept of attributing behaviour to inner character. But this can be unreliable. “Sometimes we’re in difficult positions, thrust into circumstances where we lose control or mental illness can have an effect. These things may be transient and that behaviour might not reflect upon our character,” says Dean.



Burckhardt thinks “it’s more important to who they currently are rather than do a forensic examination of their entire past.” “[But] if it’s something, extremely shocking, like they’ve committed a serious crime, then obviously I think that is very important to disclose.” Where do you draw the line? While it may not be possible to ever truly know someone, Dean says it is important to have an idea of one’s own values. “We need to ethically have an idea of ‘who I am and what are my rights? What am I willing to defend. And what are my red lines?’ That’s a part of wisdom and self-knowledge. It’s a journey that we all go on trying to learn and figure these things out for ourselves,” he says.



But beyond these hard lines, loving someone should involve a willingness to evolve. Editor's pick Opinion

Sunday Life My partner is perfect. But scratch the surface and these things bug me Kerri Sackville Columnist and author “A big part of relationships is not just meeting someone as they are, but going on a journey with someone, influencing them and allowing yourself to be influenced by them, hopefully in a mutually constructive way,” says Dean. “We are all flawed creatures, and we know that vulnerability can cause us to do irrational and sometimes harmful things.” Peel recommends having an open conversation with a partner about these lines, which helps build trust.



“It’s important to sit down and talk about, ‘OK, what are our boundaries? What’s something that we’re willing to share or talk about?’” “For example, are you willing to let your partner go through your phone? That’s where you start to establish the line between privacy and secrecy.” Even something like an affair, might not necessarily be a death sentence, she says. “That can be a catalyst for change, reflection and reanalysing what’s going on in that relationship.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter.
